newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela, rebel chief discuss Zaire peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Mandela, rebel chief discuss Zaire peace moves.

text.p: Zaire rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Wednesday he hoped direct peace talks could start soon with the government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, but it was too early to speak of a ceasefire in Zaire's civil war.

In a visit likely to boost his standing ahead of an African summit conference on the crisis, Kabila was invited to the private residence of South African President Nelson Mandela in Johannesburg for an hour of closed-door talks.

At a brief encounter with the media afterwards, together with Mandela in the garden of his home, the rebel leader said he had briefed the South African president on the situation in eastern and southern Zaire, and welcomed his advice.
"We must assume that peace can be found with the regime of Mr Mobutu," he said. "Let's hope the negotiations will start soon."
Asked if the two sides in the conflict were close to a ceasefire agreement, Kabila replied:
"Not ceasefire. We are close to a negotiation. We haven't yet discussed it with them, so that we come to a ceasefire position or other position."
He made clear he was ready for direct talks with the Mobutu government, and added: "But we haven't yet discussed it with the others what we do decide."
Kabila's rebel force, many of them Zairean Tutsis whose ethnic kin control neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi, took up arms last October and have overrun eastern Zaire's borderlands.
The conflict escalated this month with the bombing of rebel-held towns and has sent tens of thousands of refugees fleeing, threatening to destabilise Zaire and its neighbours.

Giving Kabila his military title, Mandela said: "General Laurent Kabila came down here to brief me about the situation. We are discussing very sensitive matters where confidentiality is absolutely necessary."

Kabila arrived amid great secrecy in South Africa on Tuesday, following confidential proximity talks in Cape Town on South African efforts, assisted by the United States and the United Nations, to bring the two sides together.
There has been no word from tight-lipped South African officials on what progress was made in Cape Town, if any.
Wednesday's surprise meeting was announced at the last minute and coincided with signs of an accelerating bid by African states to deal collectively with the crisis.

Kabila arrived at Mandela's home in a white minibus escorted by members of the South African Intelligence Service, and strict security was in force. Mandela took him by the arm for a tete-a-tete as he escorted him to his car later.

Their talks followed an announcement by African foreign ministers in Tripoli on Wednesday that African leaders would hold a summit conference on the situation in Central Africa on March 18-19, at a location still to be decided.
It also came hard on the heels of Mandela's return from a gathering of 18 African leaders in Botswana on Wednesday.
Diplomats said visiting U.S. Assistant Secretary of State George Moose also met Kabila on Wednesday.
Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela was committed to an early meeting with Mobutu, and would probably go to Zaire with other African leaders.
Mandela said earlier this week he hoped to meet Mobutu in Kenya or Zaire on March 19 -- a date yet to be confirmed.
